newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Single Market working, but could do better.
newsitem.headline: Single Market working, but could do better.

text.p: The European Union's single market has helped create between 300,000 and 900,000 jobs, increased the EU's income and lowered inflation, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

But the Commission, unveiling the results of 38 economic impact studies, said EU member states were still not doing enough to tap the single market's full potential to create jobs, growth and competitiveness.
"Now we can see that rather by working by faith we can work by sight. We can see concrete results," Mario Monti, the European Commissioner responsible for the market told a news conference.
"We can still do better. There are gaps to be plugged," he said, adding that the introduction of a single European currency -- planned for January 1, 1999 -- would make the market more efficient.

According to the first Commission figures on the impact of the single market for goods, services, capital and people, EU gross domestic product was 1.1-1.5 percent higher in 1994 than it would have been.
It said inflation rates were 1-1.5 percent lower than they would have been if the market had never happened.
Foreign direct investment had also been attracted to the EU by the single market, it said.
But it adds "delays in applying and enforcing single market rules at national level continue to limit the single market's positive contribution to growth, competitive and more employment."
Citing examples of the market's success, the Commission said the abolition of customs red tape had saved intra-EU traders five billion Ecus a year.

Although EU member states had a poor record when it came to applying legislation intended to open EU public markets, public purchases of non-domestic origin increased from six percent in 1987 to 10 percent of total public sector purchases in 1994.

In the car industry, the Commission said, the move from separate national systems to a single EU system for type approval had led to savings of up to 30 million Ecus for car manufacturers through a 10 per cent reduction in the cost of developing a new model.

It said telecommunications equipment prices have dropped by around seven percent between 1985 and 1995 due to single market measures, resulting in annual cost savings of between 1.5 and two billion Ecus.

It said the number of cross-border branches in the banking sector had increased between 1993 and 1995 and the price of phone calls to the United States reduced by some 42 percent between 1990 and 1995.
On the down side, the EU had made little progress on abolishing passport checks on people, harmonising taxation and creating EU rules on company law, Monti said.

He also favours powers to penalise EU member states for breaches of single market rules and said the Commission is working to simplify the legislation, through the so-called SLIM initiative, where possible.
He said just over half of the legislation necessary to make the market work was fully applied in all member states, although the figure would be 85 per cent if the record of Greece was omitted.
However the Commission said it was committed to simplifying single market legislation and vowed to crack down on member states which do not enforce the rules.
